## The question

Foundation models for time series are sold as a replacement for the feature
engineering that gradient-boosted trees need: no lags to design, no calendar to
encode, no per-series training, etc. This series tests that claim and the intuition that 
a model designed to tackle any time-series without further specification will be weaker when faced with a very unique problem.

This "hard" time-series problem is the [M5 Forecasting --- Accuracy](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/m5-forecasting-accuracy)
panel, composed of item×store series of daily Walmart sales.

M5 was chosen for two specific reasons beyond its fame - which makes comparisons all the more relevant. Chronos-2 has **no
training leakage** on it, so we can consider zero-shot predictions. And its
dynamics are mostly **endogenous**: on fev-bench the multivariate model beats
its univariate sibling by a hair (WQL 0.555 vs 0.559), which implies a
cross-series machinery has little to feed on here (which Chronos2 can be equipped with). That makes it a clean test of the model itself rather than of unfair competition over covariates one can invent around it.

## Underlying rules for the numbers

Three commitments, kept throughout:

- **Every choice is made on a validation origin** (2016-03-27) and measured once
  on a test origin (2016-04-24). Nothing is selected on the window it is scored on.
- **The evaluation roster is frozen** before any model runs, and every metric is
  reported next to the number of series it was computed on.
- **Any two numbers whose difference is interpreted share their hardware.** CPU
  and GPU disagree in the third decimal of WQL, which is enough to invert a close
  ranking, so the Chronos-2 corpus is entirely GPU and every artifact carries the
  device it was produced on.

Code and artifacts: [`m5-chronos2`](https://github.com/amelien-quenet/m5-chronos2).
